lede: Stations read against the page images of their sources only; each names its source. More will follow with the modules.

stations.text: Williston, population 100 by the gazetteer's count, has one general store, a saw and grist mill and a vegetable crate factory. The nearest railroad, express and telegraph are at Archer, eleven miles off.
stations.quelle: Florida State Gazetteer and Business Directory 1886–7, p. 458.

stations.titel: About 350 men on the line from Archer
stations.text: A trade journal reports about 350 men at work on the railway from Archer to Dunnellon, to be operated by the Florida Central & Peninsular.
stations.quelle: Engineering News, 4 July 1891, p. 20.

stations.text: The Plant System gives up its own line through the phosphate district near Albion and agrees with the Florida Central & Peninsular on the common use of the spur south of Archer.
stations.quelle: Manufacturers' Record, 30 June 1893, p. 396.

stations.titel: Leased convicts in the pits and camps
stations.text: The state's leased convicts are worked in the county: about 160 near Albion, Levy county, mining phosphate, and about fifteen sublet to Colonel H. L. Morris of Morriston for the manufacture of naval stores. Of the state's 614 prisoners at the end of 1894, 512 are Black men.
stations.quelle: Report of the Commissioner of Agriculture of the State of Florida, 1893–1894, pp. 67, 81.

stations.text: The lessee E. B. Bailey, writing from Albion, reports twenty-one deaths among the convicts in 1895 and nineteen in 1896, three of them killed while escaping or being recaptured; some of the prisoners sent to him are “not thirteen years of age”.
stations.quelle: Report of the Commissioner of Agriculture of the State of Florida, 1895–1896, p. 81.

stations.text: The act to incorporate the town is approved; the first election is set for the first Tuesday in July. In 1905 the legislature declares the incorporation lawful after the fact.
stations.quelle: Laws of Florida 1905, ch. 5550, p. 870, and ch. 5549, p. 869.

stations.text: In the season of 1897 the country around Williston grows 20,000 crates of cucumbers, worth $20,000 net to the growers.
stations.quelle: Ocala Evening Star, 16 June 1897, p. 1.

stations.text: The state's Railroad Commission lists two stations named Williston, one on each road, and the same freight from both: ten cents a crate of vegetables, sixteen a box of oranges. The charge onward to the northern markets is beyond its control.
stations.quelle: First Annual Report of the Railroad Commission of the State of Florida (1898), pp. 12–13, 43, 86, 94.

stations.text: Seven of the state's twelve convict camps, with 507 prisoners, mine phosphate; one camp in Levy County, at Elliston, is worked by W. N. Camp of Albion.
stations.quelle: Report of the Commissioner of Agriculture of the State of Florida, 1899–1900, pp. 47–48.

stations.text: A federal soil survey finds that “the principal money crop in the vicinity of Williston is cucumbers”; peanuts are grown to fatten hogs, and the orange groves were lost in 1895. Day wages in the area are 75 cents.
stations.quelle: Rice and Geib, Soil Survey of the Gainesville Area, Florida, in: Field Operations of the Bureau of Soils, 1904, pp. 278, 287.

stations.text: Wash Bradley, a Black turpentine worker accused of killing Mrs. N. B. Barrow near Levyville, is tortured and lynched by a mob near Bronson. No one is charged.
stations.quelle: Ocala Evening Star, 7 September 1904, p. 1; NAACP, Thirty Years of Lynching (1919), p. 55.

stations.text: Williston is an incorporated town on the Seaboard Air Line and the Atlantic Coast Line, with a bank, two hotels, a crate factory and a weekly paper.
stations.quelle: R. L. Polk & Co.'s Florida Gazetteer and Business Directory 1907–1908, p. 452.

stations.text: A county commissioner tells of nine cars of cucumbers shipped from Williston in one day and $29,000 received in a week.
stations.quelle: Ocala Evening Star, 12 July 1907, p. 2.

stations.text: At the height of the season Williston ships 22 cars of cucumbers a day, from about 435 acres.
stations.quelle: Florida's Financial and Industrial Record, 18 June 1910, p. 12.

stations.text: “Owing to the interruption of European shipment”, Florida's hard-rock phosphate falls from 477,538 tons (1913) to 310,267 tons; almost every ton shipped goes abroad. The state's list of phosphate companies opens with the Acme Phosphate Co. of Morriston.
stations.quelle: Florida Geological Survey, Seventh Annual Report (1915), pp. 20–22.

stations.text: The Seaboard Air Line's guide for shippers and settlers prints a photograph of a “solid trainload of cucumbers leaving Williston … destined to eastern markets”.
stations.quelle: Seaboard Air Line Railway, Shippers Guide 1914, pp. 70–71.

stations.text: “After two years of failure” the growers prosper again “in the section for which Williston is the shipping point”. Dan Warren is killed by lightning on a wagon of cucumbers at a packing house.
stations.quelle: Ocala Evening Star, 15 June 1916, p. 2.

stations.text: The hard rock fields export 12,403 tons, against 476,898 in 1913; “the export business is cut off”.
stations.quelle: Florida Geological Survey, Tenth and Eleventh Annual Reports (1918), pp. 105–106.

stations.text: Thirteen to twenty cars a day leave Williston in the peak week, mostly in solid trains on the Atlantic Coast Line; by the end of June the season's count is over 200,000 crates.
stations.quelle: Lakeland Evening Telegram, 11 and 28 June 1919.

stations.text: Herman Gunter of the state survey photographs the Acme Phosphate Company's pit five miles southwest of Morriston. In 1920 the hard rock fields market 400,249 tons, a “very decided increase”.
stations.quelle: Florida Memory GE0629; Florida Geological Survey, Fourteenth Annual Report (1922), pp. 29–30.

stations.text: On 120 farms around Williston cucumbers bring 72.3 percent of all receipts; labour is the largest expense, paid to day labourers, contract pickers and sharecroppers; two farms in five lose money.
stations.quelle: Turlington and Hamilton, Bulletin 175 (1925), pp. 5, 8, 10–11.

stations.text: Armed white men besiege a house at Rosewood and burn the Black settlement over several days; two white men and, by the official count, six Black residents are killed, among them James Carrier at his family's graves. The survivors flee into the woods.
stations.quelle: Palatka Daily News, 5, 7 and 8 January 1923 (Associated Press).

stations.text: A special grand jury at Bronson finds that “sufficient evidence had not been found” to charge anyone for the killings and the burning of Rosewood.
stations.quelle: Miami Daily Metropolis, 12 February 1923; Fort Pierce News-Tribune, 20 February 1923.
